items.label: Question 2(d)

oe.title: The chemistry of bromine
n5: Bromine is a halogen in group 7: its atoms have 7 outer electrons (2,8,18,7) and gain one electron to form the bromide ion, Br−.
It exists as diatomic Br₂ molecules held by a single covalent bond, with weak forces between molecules, so it is a liquid at room temperature (one of only two liquid elements).
It is a reactive non-metal: it forms ionic bromides with metals (e.g. NaBr, KBr) and covalent compounds with non-metals (e.g. HBr).
Isotopes: 79Br and 81Br have the same number of protons (35) but different numbers of neutrons; the relative atomic mass of 80 shows roughly equal amounts of each.
Bromine water is used to test for unsaturation: it is decolourised quickly by alkenes in an addition reaction.
It is less reactive than chlorine, so chlorine displaces bromine from bromide solutions.
higher: Down group 7, atomic size increases and electronegativity falls, so reactivity decreases (F > Cl > Br > I).
London dispersion forces increase with the number of electrons, explaining why melting and boiling points rise down the group (Cl₂ gas, Br₂ liquid, I₂ solid).
Halogens are oxidising agents: Br₂ + 2e− → 2Br−; displacement reactions are redox reactions.
Bromine radicals take part in chain reactions (initiation, propagation, termination), e.g. with alkanes in UV light.
eqns: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂ (addition: bromine water decolourised)
diagrams: Electron arrangement diagram of a bromine atom and a bromide ion.
Dot-and-cross diagram of a Br₂ molecule.
Bromine water test: test tube before (orange-brown) and after adding an alkene (colourless).

items.label: Question 12

oe.title: Identifying aluminium, iron, tin and zinc
n5: Physical tests: compare appearance, density and hardness; iron is the only magnetic metal of the four.

Reactivity with dilute acid: aluminium and zinc react readily (aluminium may be slow at first because of its oxide layer), iron reacts slowly and tin very slowly; count or compare the hydrogen bubbles.
Hydrogen can be tested with a lit splint: it burns with a pop.
Displacement reactions: a metal displaces any metal below it in the electrochemical series from a solution of its ions (e.g. zinc displaces iron and tin).
Electrochemical cells: pair each metal with a reference metal (e.g. copper) and compare voltages; metals further apart in the electrochemical series give larger voltages.
Tests on ions after reacting with acid: Fe2+/Fe3+ give coloured solutions or precipitates; precipitation with hydroxide ions can distinguish the metal ions.
Flame tests are not useful for these four metals, so other tests are needed.
higher: Use the standard reduction potentials (E°) from the data booklet to predict which displacement reactions and cell voltages will occur.
Aluminium's protective oxide layer can make it appear less reactive than expected.
Fe²⁺ can be detected with ferroxyl indicator (blue) or by oxidation with acidified potassium permanganate (decolourised).
Mass of metal and volume of hydrogen produced can be used to identify the metal through mole calculations.
diagrams: Four test tubes of each metal in the same acid, labelled with how fast bubbles form.
Simple cell with each metal and copper, connected by a voltmeter and an ion bridge.
Results table ranking the metals by voltage and by reaction with acid.

items.label: Question 6

oe.title: The role of electrons in chemistry
n5: Atoms: electrons (negative, almost no mass) are arranged in shells around the nucleus; the electron arrangement decides the group and chemical properties.
Bonding: covalent bonds are shared pairs of electrons; ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred to give ions with stable arrangements; metallic bonding involves delocalised electrons.
Conduction: metals conduct because delocalised electrons move; electrons flow through the wire in cells.
Redox: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain; ion-electron equations.
Shapes of molecules depend on bonding and non-bonding pairs (e.g. angular H₂O, pyramidal NH₃).
Beta particles are fast electrons from the nucleus.
higher: Ionisation energy: energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms; trends depend on nuclear charge and shielding.
Electronegativity and polar covalent bonds; London dispersion forces arise from temporary dipoles caused by electron movement.
Oxidising and reducing agents; electrons in flame colours (excited electrons emit light as they fall back to lower levels).
Free radicals have an unpaired electron (e.g. in chain reactions and ozone depletion).
eqns: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ (first ionisation energy, Higher)
diagrams: Electron arrangement (target) diagrams for an atom and its ion.
Dot-and-cross diagrams for a covalent molecule and an ionic compound.
Metallic lattice with delocalised electrons; cell with electron flow arrow.

items.label: Question 12

oe.title: The chemistry of sodium chloride
n5: Ionic compound: a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by strong electrostatic forces, so it has a high melting point (801 °C).
Conducts when molten or dissolved (ions free to move) but not as a solid.
Soluble in water; used as table salt, to grit roads (lowers the freezing point of water) and to preserve food.
Formed in neutralisation: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide (or carbonate) → sodium chloride + water. Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.
Electrolysis of molten NaCl gives sodium at the negative electrode and chlorine at the positive electrode.
Gives a yellow flame (sodium); chloride can be tested with silver nitrate (white precipitate of AgCl).
higher: Large electronegativity difference between Na and Cl gives ionic bonding.
Ions are smaller/larger than their atoms: Na⁺ is smaller than Na (one fewer shell); Cl⁻ is larger than Cl (more electron repulsion).
Precipitation titration / gravimetric analysis to find the chloride content.
Soaps are sodium salts of fatty acids; adding NaCl helps separate soap from solution.
eqns: Electrolysis: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na and 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
diagrams: Ionic lattice of NaCl (alternating Na⁺ and Cl⁻).
Electron arrangement diagrams for Na⁺ and Cl⁻.
Electrolysis cell for molten sodium chloride.

items.label: Question 6

oe.title: The chemistry of fertilisers
n5: Plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (N, P, K). Fertilisers replace these in the soil as crops remove them.
Fertilisers must be soluble so the ions can be absorbed through the roots (data booklet solubility table).
Ammonium and nitrate salts provide N; phosphates provide P; potassium salts provide K. Examples: ammonium nitrate NH₄NO₃, potassium phosphate K₃PO₄, ammonium phosphate (NH₄)₃PO₄.
Made by neutralisation: ammonia (from the Haber process) + nitric acid (from the Ostwald process) → ammonium nitrate.
Calculate % by mass of an element to compare fertilisers.
Problems: excess fertiliser washes into rivers and lakes (eutrophication / algal bloom).
higher: Haber process equilibrium and conditions (compromise temperature, high pressure, iron catalyst, recycling unreacted gases) to maximise yield economically.
Percentage yield and atom economy calculations for fertiliser manufacture.
Ostwald process: ammonia oxidised over a platinum catalyst; the reaction is exothermic so the catalyst stays hot.
diagrams: Flow diagram of the Haber process with a recycling loop.
Flow chart from air and natural gas to ammonia, nitric acid and ammonium nitrate.

items.label: Question 12

oe.title: Placing calcium, copper, tin and zinc in a reactivity series
n5: React each metal with water: calcium reacts (fizzing, forms an alkali); copper, tin and zinc do not.
React the rest with dilute acid (same concentration, volume, temperature and metal size): zinc fizzes steadily, tin reacts very slowly, copper does not react.
React with oxygen (heat in air / with potassium permanganate): the more reactive the metal, the more vigorous the reaction.
Displacement reactions: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from a solution of its salt (e.g. zinc + copper sulfate).
Cells: pair each metal with copper and measure the voltage; a larger voltage means more reactive.
Order: calcium > zinc > tin > copper.
higher: Use the electrochemical series / reduction potentials to explain the order; metals higher up are stronger reducing agents.
Ion-electron equations, e.g. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Measure volumes of hydrogen over time and calculate average rates to rank quantitatively.
diagrams: Test tubes of acid, each with a different metal and different amounts of bubbling.
Cell with metal X and copper electrodes and a voltmeter.
Results table comparing each test.

items.label: Question 5

oe.title: How the elements are positioned in the Periodic Table
n5: Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (number of protons). Mendeleev originally used atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements.
Columns are groups: elements in the same group have the same number of outer electrons and similar chemical properties (e.g. group 1 alkali metals, group 7 halogens, group 0 noble gases).
Rows are periods: the period number equals the number of occupied electron shells.
Metals are on the left, non-metals on the right; transition metals in the centre.
Diatomic elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂).
higher: Trends: covalent radius decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge) and increases down a group (more shells, more screening).
Ionisation energy increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Bonding and structure across period 2/3: metallic (Li, Na), covalent network (B, C, Si), covalent molecular (N₂, P₄, S₈), monatomic (noble gases), with corresponding m.p. trends.
eqns: First ionisation energy: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻ (Higher)
Group 1 reaction showing similar properties: 2Li + 2H₂O → 2LiOH + H₂ and 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂
diagrams: Outline of the periodic table labelling groups, periods, metals and non-metals.
Graph of covalent radius or first ionisation energy against atomic number.
Electron arrangement diagrams for elements in the same group.

items.label: Question 11

oe.title: Radioactive decay
n5: Unstable nuclei emit radiation to become more stable. Decay happens in the nucleus and is random.
Alpha (helium nucleus, 4/2 He): stopped by paper, positively charged. Beta (electron, 0/-1 e): stopped by thin aluminium. Gamma (electromagnetic): needs thick lead or concrete.
Alpha decay: mass number falls by 4, atomic number by 2. Beta decay: a neutron changes into a proton, so the atomic number rises by 1 and the mass number is unchanged.
Half-life: the time for half the nuclei to decay (activity to halve); it is not affected by temperature, concentration or chemical form.
Uses: medical tracers (short half-life gamma/beta), carbon-14 dating, thickness gauges, smoke detectors (alpha).
Behaviour in an electric field: alpha bends towards the negative plate, beta towards the positive plate, gamma is undeflected.
higher: Radioactivity is not part of the Higher course, but Higher calculation skills still help: fraction remaining = (1/2)^n after n half-lives.
Proportional reasoning, e.g. calculating the mass of an isotope left or the age of a sample.
eqns: After 3 half-lives: 1/2 x 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/8 remains; 20 g → 2.5 g
diagrams: Paper, aluminium and lead blocking alpha, beta and gamma.
Paths of alpha, beta and gamma between charged plates.
Decay curve of activity against time with half-lives marked.

items.label: Question 5

oe.title: The chemistry of nitrogen
n5: Nitrogen is in group 5 (2,5) and exists as diatomic N₂ molecules with a triple covalent bond, which makes it very unreactive.
Covalent molecular gas with weak forces between molecules, so a very low boiling point.
Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ using an iron catalyst. Ammonia is used to make fertilisers and nitric acid (Ostwald process, platinum catalyst).
Nitrogen is an essential element for plant growth (N, P, K); fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate supply it.
Nitrogen oxides form in car engines (spark) and dissolve in rain to form acid rain.
Ammonia (NH₃) is trigonal pyramidal and dissolves to give an alkaline solution.
higher: Haber process equilibrium: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a compromise temperature (~450 °C) and high pressure are used; unreacted gases are recycled (Le Chatelier).
N is highly electronegative, so N-H bonds are polar and ammonia molecules form hydrogen bonds (high boiling point for its size).
Proteins contain nitrogen in the amide (peptide) link -CONH-; amino acids contain the amine group -NH₂.
The triple bond has a very high bond enthalpy (945 kJ mol⁻¹ in the data booklet), explaining nitrogen's lack of reactivity.
diagrams: Dot-and-cross diagram of N₂ showing the triple bond.
Flow diagram of the Haber process with a recycle loop.
Shape of NH₃ (trigonal pyramidal).

items.label: Question 12

oe.title: Investigating one factor that affects the rate of reaction
n5: Choose one factor: concentration of acid, temperature, particle size (surface area) of marble, or a catalyst. Change only that factor; keep everything else constant.
Measure: volume of CO₂ against time (gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder), loss in mass on a balance, or the time for the reaction to finish.
Calculate average rate = change in quantity / change in time and compare; repeat for reliability.
Expected result: higher concentration, higher temperature, smaller chips (larger surface area) all increase the rate because there are more collisions between particles.
Plot a graph of volume or mass against time for each condition.
higher: Collision theory: particles must collide with energy ≥ activation energy (Ea) and with the correct orientation.
Temperature: a small rise greatly increases the number of particles with energy ≥ Ea (energy distribution diagram), so the rate increases significantly.
Use relative rate = 1/t to compare experiments.
Calculate the moles of CO₂ from its volume using molar volume.
eqns: Average rate = (60 - 20) cm³ / (40 - 10) s = 1.33 cm³ s⁻¹
diagrams: Flask with marble chips and acid connected to a gas syringe; or flask with cotton wool on a balance.
Sketch graph comparing two experiments: steeper curve for the faster rate.
Energy distribution curve at two temperatures, with Ea marked.

items.label: Question 5

oe.title: Which indigestion tablet is most effective?
n5: Neutralisation: base + acid → salt + water (+ CO₂ for carbonates). The better tablet neutralises more acid.
Method 1: dissolve one tablet of each brand and titrate with hydrochloric acid of known concentration using an indicator; the brand needing more acid is more effective.
Method 2: add one tablet to a fixed volume and concentration of acid; measure the pH after reaction (higher pH = more acid neutralised).
Method 3: add powdered tablet in portions to the acid until the pH reaches 7, or until fizzing stops, and compare the mass needed.
Method 4: collect the volume of CO₂ produced from each tablet.
Fair test: same mass/number of tablets, acid volume and concentration, temperature; crush both to the same particle size.
higher: Back titration: add excess acid of known amount, then titrate the leftover acid with standard NaOH to find how much the tablet neutralised.
Calculate moles of acid neutralised (n = cV) and mass of CaCO₃ using the mole ratio 1:2.
Mole ratio and excess: identify the limiting reactant.
diagrams: Titration apparatus with the dissolved tablet in the conical flask.
Beaker of acid with pH meter as tablet is added.
Graph of pH against mass of tablet added.

items.label: Question 13

oe.title: The chemistry of redox reactions
n5: Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain of electrons (OIL RIG). Both happen together in a redox reaction.
Ion-electron equations show each half; electrons lost must equal electrons gained when combining them.
Examples: metals reacting with acids, displacement reactions, extraction of metals (reduction of metal ions), electrolysis, and electrochemical cells.
In a cell, electrons flow through the wire from the metal higher in the electrochemical series (oxidised) to the lower one; the ion bridge completes the circuit.
Electrolysis: reduction at the negative electrode, oxidation at the positive electrode.
higher: Oxidising agents accept electrons (e.g. halogens, acidified permanganate and dichromate); reducing agents donate electrons (e.g. reactive metals).
Writing complex ion-electron equations with H⁺ and H₂O, e.g. Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Oxidation of organic compounds: primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; antioxidants are reducing agents that prevent oxidation of food.
Redox titrations: permanganate is self-indicating.
eqns: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻  and  Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu
diagrams: Two half-cells joined by an ion bridge and voltmeter, with electron flow arrow through the wire.
Electrolysis cell labelling oxidation and reduction at each electrode.

items.label: Question 5

oe.title: Chemical reactions and properties of metals
n5: Metallic bonding: lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, so metals conduct electricity (solid and liquid) and heat, are malleable and generally have high m.p.
Reactions with oxygen, water and dilute acid, used to build the reactivity series (e.g. K, Na react with water; Cu does not react with dilute acid).
Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen; metal + oxygen → metal oxide.
Extraction depends on reactivity: electrolysis (Al, Na), heating with carbon (Fe, Zn), heat alone (Ag, Hg). Extraction is reduction.
Electrochemical cells: two different metals in an electrolyte give a voltage; electrons flow from the more reactive metal.
Metals form positive ions and ionic compounds; displacement reactions.
higher: Metals are reducing agents: they lose electrons (are oxidised). Group 1 metals are the strongest reducing agents.
First ionisation energy decreases down a group (larger atoms, more shielding), so reactivity of group 1 and 2 metals increases.
Metallic elements in the periodic table: metallic lattice structures; transition metals and their ions used as catalysts (Fe in Haber, Pt in Ostwald).
Using a reduction potential table to predict which reactions occur.
eqns: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu (ionic: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu)
diagrams: Metallic lattice with + ions and delocalised electrons.
Simple cell with electron flow direction through the wire.
Electrolysis of a molten metal compound.

items.label: Question 13

oe.title: Which vinegar has the highest concentration of ethanoic acid?
n5: Titration is the most accurate method: pipette a fixed volume (e.g. 20 cm³) of each vinegar into a conical flask, add indicator (e.g. phenolphthalein), and titrate with standard sodium hydroxide from a burette.
Repeat until concordant titres (within 0.2 cm³) are obtained and average them; the vinegar needing the largest titre is the most concentrated.
Calculate the concentration using moles: n = cV and the mole ratio 1:1.
Alternatives: measure pH (lower pH = more H⁺), react with the same mass of a carbonate or magnesium and compare rates or volume of gas, or measure the temperature rise on neutralisation.
Fair test: same volume of each vinegar and same temperature.
higher: Ethanoic acid is a weak acid (only partially ionised), so pH is a poorer comparison than titration, which reacts all of the acid.
Volumetric analysis with a standard solution; dilute strong vinegars accurately with a volumetric flask before titrating.
Calculate % ethanoic acid by mass from the concentration (GFM of CH₃COOH = 60).
diagrams: Labelled titration apparatus: burette (NaOH), pipette, conical flask with vinegar and indicator, white tile.
Results table showing rough and concordant titres.

items.label: Question 6

oe.title: The chemistry of oxides
n5: Metal oxides are bases. Soluble metal oxides (e.g. Na₂O, CaO) dissolve to form alkaline solutions (pH above 7).
Non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₂, NO₂) dissolve to form acidic solutions; SO₂ and NO₂ cause acid rain.
Metal oxides neutralise acids: metal oxide + acid → salt + water.
Bonding: metal oxides are ionic lattices (high m.p., conduct when molten); many non-metal oxides are covalent molecular gases (CO₂), but SiO₂ is a covalent network.
Metals are extracted from oxide ores: heat alone (Ag₂O, HgO), heating with carbon / CO (Fe₂O₃, CuO), or electrolysis (Al₂O₃).
Combustion produces oxides: carbon dioxide and water from hydrocarbons; incomplete combustion gives toxic carbon monoxide.
higher: Across period 3 the oxides change from basic ionic (Na₂O, MgO) to acidic covalent (SO₂); Al₂O₃ is amphoteric.
Extraction is a reduction: metal ions gain electrons; the carbon monoxide is the reducing agent.
Oxidising agents such as oxygen gain electrons; oxide ions are O²⁻.
Bond enthalpy calculations can estimate the energy released forming C=O and O-H bonds in combustion.
diagrams: pH scale showing metal oxides as alkaline and non-metal oxides as acidic.
Ionic lattice for MgO and a molecule diagram for CO₂ (linear).
Blast furnace or electrolysis cell for extraction from the oxide.

items.label: Question 13

oe.title: Why the attraction between opposite charges matters
n5: Atoms: negative electrons are held around the positive nucleus by this attraction.
Ionic bonding: the electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions holds the lattice together, giving high melting points.
Covalent bonding: a shared pair of electrons is attracted to both positive nuclei.
Metallic bonding: positive ions attracted to delocalised electrons.
Electrolysis: positive ions move to the negative electrode and negative ions to the positive electrode.
Ion bridge / cells: ions move to balance charge as electrons flow through the wire.
higher: Intermolecular forces: London dispersion forces (temporary dipoles), permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions and hydrogen bonding are all attractions between opposite partial charges (delta+ / delta-).
Electronegativity: the attraction an atom has for the electrons in a bond; differences cause polar covalent bonds.
Trends: nuclear charge increases across a period, pulling electrons closer, so covalent radius decreases and ionisation energy increases.
Chromatography separates molecules partly by polarity: polar molecules are attracted to a polar stationary phase.
eqns: Electrolysis of CuCl₂: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (negative electrode); 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (positive electrode)
diagrams: Atom diagram with nucleus and electron shells.
Ionic lattice of NaCl; covalent bond showing shared pair between two nuclei; metallic lattice.
Electrolysis cell with ions migrating to the oppositely charged electrodes.
Two polar molecules (e.g. HCl) with delta+ / delta- labels and a dotted line between them.

items.label: Question 8

oe.title: The chemistry of water
n5: Covalent molecular compound H₂O: angular (bent) shape; each O-H is a covalent bond.
Good solvent: dissolves ionic compounds (ions free to move) and is used to make solutions.
Neutral (pH 7): contains equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻; dilution moves acids and alkalis towards pH 7.
Product of neutralisation and of combustion of hydrocarbons and alcohols; tested with cobalt chloride paper (blue to pink).
Reacts with reactive metals (e.g. sodium) to form alkali + hydrogen; soluble metal oxides and non-metal oxides react with water to form alkalis and acids.
Used in hydration (alkene + water → alcohol) and as the coolant/heat absorber in E = cmΔT experiments (c = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹).
higher: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules (polar O-H bonds, permanent dipoles) explains its unusually high boiling point and why ice is less dense than water.
O is more electronegative than H, so the O-H bonds are polar and the molecule is polar overall.
Hydrolysis: water breaks esters, fats and proteins apart; condensation reactions release water.
Water acts as both acid and base: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻ (dynamic equilibrium).
diagrams: Dot-and-cross diagram of H₂O showing two bonding pairs and two non-bonding pairs; angular shape.
Hydrogen bonds drawn as dotted lines between water molecules (delta+ H to delta- O).
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions surrounded by water molecules when dissolving.

items.label: Question 17

oe.title: The chemistry of methacrylic acid
n5: Carboxylic acid: contains the carboxyl group (-COOH), so it forms an acidic solution (pH below 7).
Reacts as an acid with metals, bases and carbonates to form salts (methacrylates), e.g. sodium methacrylate.
Contains a C=C double bond, so it is unsaturated: decolourises bromine solution quickly and takes part in addition reactions (e.g. with hydrogen, bromine, water).
It can undergo addition polymerisation to form poly(methacrylic acid), as in nail polish.
Molecular formula C₄H₆O₂; it has isomers.
Reacts with an alcohol to form an ester (methacrylates are esters).
higher: Esterification is a condensation reaction: acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water, catalysed by concentrated sulfuric acid; the ester has a -COO- (ester link).
Methyl methacrylate polymerises to make Perspex (PMMA).
The -COOH group allows hydrogen bonding, so the acid has a relatively high boiling point and is soluble in water.
Addition polymerisation proceeds via free radicals (initiation, propagation, termination).
diagrams: Full structural formula with the carboxyl group and the C=C circled and labelled.
Section of the addition polymer showing three monomer units, with the repeating unit bracketed.
Structure of the ester formed with methanol, ester link circled.

oe.title: Investigating copper as a catalyst for zinc and sulfuric acid
n5: Run two experiments: zinc + sulfuric acid without copper, and with copper. Keep the mass and particle size of zinc, the acid volume, concentration and temperature the same.
Measure the rate: volume of hydrogen collected over time (gas syringe), or time for the zinc to react, or loss in mass.
If copper is a catalyst, the reaction with copper is faster.
Weigh the copper before and after; a catalyst is recovered chemically unchanged, so the mass stays the same.
Check copper on its own does not react with dilute sulfuric acid (copper is below hydrogen).
higher: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.
Copper and zinc in contact form a simple cell: electrons flow from zinc to copper and hydrogen is released at the copper surface, so the rate increases.
Heterogeneous catalyst: the catalyst (solid) is in a different state from the reactants (solution).
eqns: Rate = 60 cm³ / 30 s = 2 cm³ s⁻¹ (example of comparing average rates)

items.label: Question 15

oe.title: Distinguishing 0.1 and 0.2 mol l⁻¹ sodium carbonate
n5: Titration: titrate the same volume of each with acid of known concentration and an indicator. The 0.2 mol l⁻¹ solution needs about double the volume of acid.
Reaction rate: add the same acid; the more concentrated carbonate reacts faster (more collisions) and gives more CO₂.
Collect and measure the CO₂ formed with excess acid: the 0.2 mol l⁻¹ solution gives twice the volume.
pH: sodium carbonate solutions are alkaline; the more concentrated one has a higher pH.
Precipitation: add excess calcium chloride; the 0.2 mol l⁻¹ solution forms twice the mass of calcium carbonate precipitate (filter, dry and weigh).
Conductivity: the more concentrated solution has more ions and conducts better.
Evaporate equal volumes to dryness: the 0.2 mol l⁻¹ solution leaves twice the mass of solid.
higher: Volumetric calculation using concordant titres and the mole ratio (Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2).
Gravimetric analysis: heat to constant mass to ensure all water is removed before weighing.
Molar volume: convert CO₂ volume to moles to confirm the ratio of concentrations.
eqns: Mass from evaporation: 0.005 mol x 106 g mol⁻¹ = 0.53 g (25 cm³ of 0.2 mol l⁻¹)
diagrams: Titration apparatus with burette, pipette and conical flask.
Filtration set-up for collecting the precipitate.

items.label: Question 7

oe.title: The chemistry of strontium
n5: Strontium is a group 2 metal (alkaline earth metal), atomic number 38: 38 protons and 38 electrons, electron arrangement ending in 2 outer electrons.
It loses its 2 outer electrons to form Sr²⁺ ions, which have a stable noble gas arrangement; it forms ionic compounds, e.g. strontium chloride SrCl₂.
Metallic bonding: positive ions and delocalised electrons, so it conducts electricity.
Strontium salts give a red flame colour, used in fireworks and flares.
Reactive metal: reacts with water to give strontium hydroxide (alkaline) and hydrogen; extracted by electrolysis.
Strontium-90 is a radioactive isotope (beta emitter) found in nuclear fallout.
higher: Going down group 2, atomic size (covalent radius) increases because of extra electron shells, so first ionisation energy decreases and reactivity increases.
First and second ionisation energies: Sr(g) → Sr⁺(g) + e⁻ and Sr⁺(g) → Sr²⁺(g) + e⁻; a big jump at the third shows two outer electrons.
Strontium is a strong reducing agent (it is oxidised readily).
Flame colours arise from electrons being excited to higher energy levels and emitting light of specific wavelengths as they fall back.
eqns: Sr-90 → Y-90 + beta (mass 90 unchanged, atomic number 38 → 39)
diagrams: Target diagram of a strontium ion showing a full outer shell.
Ionic lattice of SrCl₂ (alternating positive and negative ions).
Graph of ionisation energy or covalent radius down group 2.

items.label: Question 13

oe.title: Which carbonated water contains more dissolved CO2?
n5: Use the same volume of each brand at the same temperature for a fair test.
Collect the gas released: warm or shake each sample and collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder; more volume means more dissolved CO₂.
Loss in mass: place the open bottle on a balance and record the mass lost as CO₂ escapes.
Measure pH: CO₂ dissolves to form an acid, so the lower pH contains more CO₂.
Titration: titrate each sample with sodium hydroxide of known concentration using an indicator; larger titre means more dissolved CO₂.
Confirm the gas is CO₂: it turns limewater cloudy.
higher: Gas solubility decreases as temperature rises, so heating drives the CO₂ out.
Equilibrium: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) and CO₂(aq) + H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Opening the bottle lowers pressure and the equilibrium shifts to release gas.
Volumetric analysis: use concordant titres (within 0.2 cm³) and n = cV with the mole ratio to calculate the CO₂ concentration.
Molar volume: convert gas volume to moles (n = V / Vm).
diagrams: Flask of carbonated water, heated gently, connected to a gas syringe.
Titration set-up: burette of NaOH above a conical flask with sample and indicator.
Bottle on an electronic balance.

items.label: Question 10

oe.title: Identifying aluminium, iron, tin and zinc
n5: Use reactivity: react each metal with dilute acid (same concentration, volume and size of strip) and compare the rate of bubbling of hydrogen. Reactivity: Al > Zn > Fe > Sn (Al may look slow at first because of its oxide layer).
Test the gas: hydrogen burns with a pop.
Build cells: pair each metal with copper in an electrolyte and measure the voltage. The further apart in the electrochemical series, the bigger the voltage.
Displacement: a metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt (e.g. zinc in tin(II) sulfate gives a coating of tin).
Other properties: density or magnetism (iron is magnetic); flame tests on the salts formed.
higher: Use reduction potentials / the electrochemical series to predict the cell voltage and the direction of electron flow (from the metal higher in the series).
Write the ion-electron equations for each metal being oxidised, e.g. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, and identify each metal as a reducing agent.
Measure the rate of hydrogen production quantitatively (gas syringe) and calculate average rates to rank the metals.
eqns: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂;  Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂
Average rate = volume of H₂ / time, e.g. 30 cm³ / 60 s = 0.5 cm³ s⁻¹
diagrams: Four test tubes of acid with a metal strip in each, showing different amounts of bubbling.
Simple cell: metal and copper electrodes in electrolyte joined through a voltmeter, with electron flow arrow through the wire.
Table of predicted results for each metal.

oe.title: Identifying three carbon-containing compounds
n5: Assume typical compounds, e.g. an alkane, an alkene and a carbonate (or an alcohol / carboxylic acid). State the tests and the expected results.
Bromine test: an alkene (unsaturated, C=C) decolourises orange/brown bromine solution quickly; an alkane does not.
A carbonate fizzes with acid giving CO₂, which turns limewater cloudy.
pH: a carboxylic acid gives pH below 7; alcohols and hydrocarbons are neutral.
Solubility: short-chain alcohols and acids dissolve in water; hydrocarbons are insoluble.
Burning: all burn to give CO₂ and water (if they contain hydrogen); test the products with limewater and cobalt chloride paper.
higher: Oxidation of alcohols: primary and secondary alcohols turn acidified potassium dichromate from orange to green; tertiary alcohols do not.
Aldehydes give a positive test with Fehling's or Tollens' reagent (blue to brick-red; silver mirror); ketones do not.
Esters have a fruity smell and are made by condensation of an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.
Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups (e.g. O-H, C=O) from absorption wavenumbers in the data booklet.
diagrams: Full structural formulae of the compounds being identified, with functional groups circled.

items.label: Question 6

oe.title: Determining the rate of the permanganate / oxalic acid reaction
n5: Rate = change in quantity / change in time. Something must be measured that changes as the reaction goes on.
Colour: purple MnO₄⁻ is turned colourless (Mn²⁺ is very pale). Time how long the purple colour takes to disappear; rate is proportional to 1/time.
Gas: CO₂ is produced, so measure its volume against time (gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder) or measure the loss in mass on a balance as CO₂ escapes.
Keep everything else the same (volumes, concentrations, temperature) for a fair test; repeat and average.
Plot volume (or mass lost) against time; the gradient of the line gives the rate, and it slows as reactants are used up.
higher: Relative rate = 1/t (s⁻¹): Higher uses this to compare rates from 'time for colour change' experiments.
This reaction is slow at room temperature and is usually warmed (about 60 °C): more particles then have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy (Ea).
The reaction is autocatalysed: the Mn²⁺ ions formed act as a catalyst, so the rate speeds up after an initial slow start.
Permanganate is self-indicating in redox titrations, which is why the colour change is so easy to see.
eqns: Average rate = change in volume / change in time, e.g. 40 cm³ / 20 s = 2 cm³ s⁻¹
Relative rate = 1/t, e.g. colour gone in 25 s gives 1/25 = 0.04 s⁻¹
diagrams: Conical flask with delivery tube to a gas syringe (or upturned measuring cylinder in water).
Flask with cotton wool plug on a top-pan balance, showing mass decreasing.
Graph of volume of CO₂ against time, steep at first then levelling off.
Energy distribution curve showing more particles above Ea at a higher temperature.

items.label: Question 14

oe.title: Could an aluminium boat dissolve in a volcanic lake?
n5: HCl, SO₂ and SO₃ are non-metal compounds that dissolve in water to form acids (hydrochloric, sulfurous and sulfuric acid), lowering the pH.
Aluminium is a reactive metal (above hydrogen) so in theory it reacts with acid: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen.
Heat from the volcano raises the temperature, increasing the rate of reaction.
However, aluminium is protected by a thin, unreactive oxide layer, so it reacts slowly at first. A thick boat would take far longer than a short crossing to develop holes.
Judgement: the reaction is possible chemically, but the speed shown in the film is unlikely.
higher: Collision theory: higher temperature gives more collisions with energy ≥ Ea; higher H⁺ concentration gives more frequent successful collisions.
Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) is amphoteric and is attacked by acid once the acid is concentrated and hot, exposing fresh metal.
Redox: aluminium is oxidised (Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻) and H⁺ is reduced (2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂). Al is the reducing agent.
Acid rain chemistry: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ and SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄.
diagrams: Particle diagram of aluminium metal with an oxide layer on the surface.
Energy distribution curve at two temperatures to explain faster reaction in hot water.
pH scale showing the lake water as acidic.
